title: Correlated errors at the failure tail: do the strongest models err together most?
quick_reasoning: Replicates counterintuitive correlated-error scaling result, directly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Correlated errors at the failure tail: do the strongest models err together most?

**Problem:** Recent work (Correlated Errors in LLMs, arXiv 2506.07962) reports that larger, more accurate models have MORE correlated errors despite distinct providers — counterintuitive and safety-relevant. This surprising result deserves an independent, scoped replication on a fresh task suite.

**Direction:** Pick a multiple-choice safety/factual benchmark (e.g., a safety-knowledge subset, TruthfulQA-style items). Score 8-10 models spanning capability levels. For each pair, compute the conditional probability that both err on the same item vs. an independence baseline; regress error-correlation on average accuracy to test whether 'better models err together more'.

**Why it matters:** If capability gains import correlated errors, scaling makes ensembles and cross-checks *less* protective exactly as stakes rise. This is a counterintuitive, infrastructure-free finding worth confirming and communicating.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Correlated Errors in LLMs (arXiv 2506.07962). Pure inference + statistics on a single GPU / API calls.

title: Jailbreak transfer as a homogeneity meter: mapping shared vulnerability across an open-model family tree
quick_reasoning: Uses jailbreak transfer to audit shared attack surface/homogeneity, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Jailbreak transfer as a homogeneity meter: mapping shared vulnerability across an open-model family tree

**Problem:** Jailbreak transferability is argued to emerge from shared representations (arXiv 2506.12913). If true, the degree to which a jailbreak transfers between two models is a *behavioral measure of their homogeneity*. No one has used transfer rate as a similarity metric across a known lineage of open models.

**Direction:** Take a set of open models with known lineage (base + several fine-tunes/distillations, plus unrelated families). Use a small bank of published jailbreak prompts. Measure pairwise jailbreak transfer success and build a 'vulnerability dendrogram'. Test whether transfer rate tracks known lineage and whether shared base = shared vulnerability.

**Why it matters:** Provides a cheap, training-free probe for hidden model homogeneity that downstream deployers could use to audit whether their 'diverse' model pool actually shares attack surface — relevant to concentration risk monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (arXiv 2506.12913) and the systemic reuse vulnerability framing. Uses public jailbreak prompts and open models only.

title: The distilled-monoculture hypothesis: do high-distillation models share more failures?
quick_reasoning: Tests distillation-driven correlated failure (concentration risk), well targeted.

original_idea.body:
# The distilled-monoculture hypothesis: do high-distillation models share more failures?

**Problem:** Distillation-quantification work (arXiv 2501.12619) estimates that many open and closed models have high 'distillation degree' (sharing a teacher), while Claude/Gemini stand apart. If distillation drives homogeneity, high-distillation models should fail on the same items more than low-distillation ones — an untested prediction.

**Direction:** Group ~10 models into 'high-distillation' (likely sharing GPT-style teachers) vs. 'distinct lineage' clusters using the published distillation estimates. On a fixed error-prone benchmark, measure within-cluster vs. across-cluster error correlation. Test whether distillation lineage predicts correlated failure.

**Why it matters:** If distillation silently couples failure modes, the apparent diversity of the open-model ecosystem is overstated, and concentration risk hides behind nominally independent models. This is exactly the systemic-risk signal regulators want to monitor.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Quantification of LLM Distillation (arXiv 2501.12619) and Correlated Errors (2506.07962). Inference + correlation analysis on a consumer GPU.

title: Do Jailbreaks Lobotomize? Measuring Capability Tax of Successful Attacks
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reframing of jailbreak robustness via capability tax, core adversarial-robustness problem.

original_idea.body:
# Do Jailbreaks Lobotomize? Measuring Capability Tax of Successful Attacks

**Problem:** StrongREJECT found that jailbreaks which bypass safety fine-tuning tend to reduce the model's capabilities, but this 'capability tax' has not been systematically measured as a function of attack type, raising the question of whether some attacks elicit harmful but useless output.

**Direction:** For a fixed open model, apply several jailbreaks (prefill, refusal-direction ablation, many-shot, low-resource translation) and measure post-jailbreak performance on neutral capability benchmarks (GSM8K subset, MMLU subset) administered within the jailbroken context. Compare each attack's capability degradation against its StrongREJECT willingness score.

**Why it matters:** If the strongest willingness-inducing attacks also cause the most capability loss, the real-world threat is overstated and benchmarks should report a willingness-vs-capability tradeoff. This reframes how robustness is evaluated — a diffuse, fuzzy-reward measurement problem ideal for outside-lab work, needing no training.

**Relevant context:** StrongREJECT (Souly et al., arXiv:2402.10260, NeurIPS 2024): jailbreaks bypassing safety fine-tuning tend to reduce capabilities; prior evaluators overstate effectiveness by ignoring response quality. The capability tax per attack type and its correlation with willingness is unmeasured.

title: Family bias in LLM-as-judge: a self-favoring monoculture stress test for evaluation pipelines
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets self-favoring bias distorting safety evals/oversight, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Family bias in LLM-as-judge: a self-favoring monoculture stress test for evaluation pipelines

**Problem:** LLM judges favor their own and same-family outputs (self-preference and family bias; arXiv 2410.21819). Safety pipelines increasingly use one model family both to generate and to judge. If the judge systematically inflates same-family safety outputs, automated safety evals are silently biased toward the provider's own model.

**Direction:** Generate responses to a fixed safety-eval prompt set from 4-6 model families. Have each family's model judge ALL responses on a safety rubric. Compute the same-family score inflation (judge's rating of own-family vs. cross-family, controlling for an external human/aggregate gold). Quantify how much a monoculture eval setup distorts safety rankings.

**Why it matters:** Concentration on one provider for both generation and evaluation creates a self-grading loop that overstates safety. Demonstrating the size of this bias warns deployers against single-vendor safety eval stacks — a counterfactually valuable audit needing no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2410.21819) and family-bias findings. Uses API/open models and a public safety rubric; no training.

title: Verifier-ensemble illusion: how much redundancy do you actually buy from N 'independent' safety checkers?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped effective-independence metric for safety verifier ensembles, clear relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Verifier-ensemble illusion: how much redundancy do you actually buy from N 'independent' safety checkers?

**Problem:** Multi-model safety checks assume independence, but behavioral-entanglement audits (arXiv 2604.07650) show ostensibly independent models share synchronized failures. Practitioners size redundancy by counting models, not by their effective independence.

**Direction:** Build a small harness where N models each act as a binary safety classifier on a labeled harmful/benign prompt set. Estimate each pair's failure correlation, then compute the 'effective number of independent verifiers' (e.g., via the correlation-adjusted variance reduction) vs. the naive count N. Show how much the safety guarantee shrinks once correlation is accounted for.

**Why it matters:** Gives deployers a concrete, reusable formula+notebook to discount redundancy claims when their verifiers are homogeneous. Directly operationalizes the 'monitoring concentration risk across systems' open problem as a small infrastructure prototype.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on the behavioral-entanglement auditing framework (arXiv 2604.07650) and ensemble-diversity literature. Pure classification + statistics on a single GPU.

title: Intra-model repetition as a hidden mode-collapse failure: measuring 'idea exhaustion' under resampling
quick_reasoning: Diversity ceiling limits best-of-N safety mechanisms, well targeted safety implication.

original_idea.body:
# Intra-model repetition as a hidden mode-collapse failure: measuring 'idea exhaustion' under resampling

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper documents intra-model repetition (one model keeps producing similar responses). The safety failure this implies — a model that exhausts its idea space after a few samples — is not quantified as a function of sample count, which matters for any safety process relying on diverse resampling (best-of-N, self-critique).

**Direction:** For each of several open models, resample K=50 outputs per open-ended/safety prompt at fixed temperature. Plot the growth of distinct semantic clusters (via embedding clustering) as K increases; fit a saturation curve and report the 'effective diversity ceiling'. Compare across models and prompt types.

**Why it matters:** If resampling saturates after ~5 ideas, best-of-N and diversity-based safety mechanisms hit a hard ceiling. Quantifying the ceiling tells safety engineers when more samples stop buying coverage — a clean, communicable finding.

**Relevant context:** Direct follow-up to the intra-model repetition result in Artificial Hivemind. Embedding clustering and resampling run on a consumer GPU.

title: Shared hallucination: do independent models hallucinate the SAME false facts?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets correlated hallucination breaking agreement-based verification, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Shared hallucination: do independent models hallucinate the SAME false facts?

**Problem:** Homogeneity research focuses on style/refusals, but the most dangerous shared blind spot is shared *false confidence*. If models trained on overlapping corpora hallucinate identical wrong answers, cross-model agreement (a common reliability heuristic) becomes a false safety signal.

**Direction:** Use a set of questions designed to elicit hallucinations (obscure or fabricated entities, plausible-but-false claims). Query 8-10 models. Among incorrect answers, measure the rate at which multiple models give the *same wrong* answer vs. independently different wrong answers (string/semantic match). Quantify 'correlated hallucination'.

**Why it matters:** Agreement-based verification (asking several models and trusting consensus) silently fails when models share hallucinations. Demonstrating correlated hallucinations undermines a widely used cheap safety heuristic — high counterfactual value, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Connects correlated-error findings (2506.07962) to hallucination; uses TruthfulQA-style and fabricated-entity prompts. Inference + matching only.

title: Position and ordering blind spots shared across models: a correlated-bias incident study
quick_reasoning: Shared exploitable position/order biases across models, safety-relevant systemic fragility.

original_idea.body:
# Position and ordering blind spots shared across models: a correlated-bias incident study

**Problem:** Many models share systematic biases (e.g., position bias in multiple-choice, ordering bias in pairwise comparison). If these biases are correlated across vendors, a single adversarial reordering can flip decisions in every model at once — a shared exploitable failure mode.

**Direction:** On a fixed MCQ and pairwise-preference set, permute answer positions/order across models. Measure each model's position-bias magnitude and direction, then test whether biases are correlated across models (same option letter / same position favored). Estimate the fraction of items where a single reorder flips ALL models the same way.

**Why it matters:** Shared, predictable input-format biases mean an attacker needs to craft only one manipulation to fool a diverse model pool — directly demonstrating correlated, exploitable failure. Cheap to run, broadly relevant to eval and agentic safety.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on documented position/order biases in LLM evaluation and the correlated-failure framing. Public benchmarks + inference only.

title: Tokenizer-shared failures: do models with the same tokenizer family break on the same inputs?
quick_reasoning: Mechanistic source of correlated failures via shared tokenizers, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Tokenizer-shared failures: do models with the same tokenizer family break on the same inputs?

**Problem:** Homogeneity may have a low-level cause: shared tokenizers. Models using the same tokenizer (e.g., GPT-style BPE, Llama tokenizer) may share tokenization-induced failures (number splitting, rare-character glitches, 'glitch tokens'). Whether failure modes cluster by tokenizer is untested as a homogeneity driver.

**Direction:** Assemble inputs known to stress tokenization (long numbers, unusual unicode, glitch-token candidates). Group open models by tokenizer lineage. Measure failure rates and test whether same-tokenizer models fail on the same specific inputs more than cross-tokenizer pairs.

**Why it matters:** Identifies a concrete, mechanistic source of correlated failures that propagates across every model sharing a tokenizer — a supply-chain-style monoculture risk deployers never check. Fully open-model, no training.

**Relevant context:** Connects model_homogeneity 'shared blind spots' to tokenizer reuse; uses open models with documented tokenizers. Inference only on a consumer GPU.

title: When does diversity collapse? Mapping the temperature/decoding boundary of inter-model homogeneity
quick_reasoning: Boundary conditions for cheaply recovering safety-relevant diversity, well targeted.

original_idea.body:
# When does diversity collapse? Mapping the temperature/decoding boundary of inter-model homogeneity

**Problem:** Inter-model homogeneity is usually measured at default settings, but it is a boundary-condition question: at what decoding configuration (temperature, top-p) does homogeneity appear or vanish? Knowing the boundary tells us whether diversity can be cheaply recovered by sampling.

**Direction:** Hold prompts fixed; sweep temperature and top-p across several open models. At each setting measure inter-model pairwise similarity and intra-model diversity. Find the boundary where outputs stop converging, and test whether high-temperature 'diversity' is genuine (semantically distinct) or just surface noise.

**Why it matters:** If safety-relevant diversity can be recovered by turning up temperature, that is a cheap mitigation; if homogeneity is decoding-invariant, the problem is deeper. Either result is an actionable, communicable boundary-condition finding.

**Relevant context:** Boundary-condition extension of Artificial Hivemind diversity metrics. Pure sampling + embedding analysis on a single GPU.

title: Cascading-failure simulation: how one shared model's blind spot propagates through a multi-agent pipeline
quick_reasoning: Reproducible cascading-failure demo for monoculture pipelines, recognized safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Cascading-failure simulation: how one shared model's blind spot propagates through a multi-agent pipeline

**Problem:** The International AI Safety Report 2026 flags cascading failures when critical systems depend on the same foundation model. There is no small, reproducible demonstration of how a single shared blind spot amplifies through a chained pipeline (generator -> checker -> summarizer all using the same backbone).

**Direction:** Build a toy 3-stage agent pipeline where stages share vs. differ in backbone model. Inject a known shared blind spot (a prompt all instances of model A mishandle). Measure end-to-end failure rate when all stages use A vs. when stages use distinct models. Quantify the cascade amplification from monoculture.

**Why it matters:** Turns the abstract 'cascading failure' open problem into a concrete, reproducible micro-demonstration that deployers and policymakers can understand. Builds a small reusable harness for monoculture stress-testing — strategically valuable infrastructure at prototype scale.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on International AI Safety Report 2026 cascading-failure concern. Small agent harness + open models on a consumer GPU; no training.

title: Does instruction-tuning on shared data erase diversity? A before/after homogeneity comparison
quick_reasoning: Tests alignment-as-homogenization root cause, safety-relevant tension between safety tuning and diversity.

original_idea.body:
# Does instruction-tuning on shared data erase diversity? A before/after homogeneity comparison

**Problem:** A surprising-result hypothesis: base (pretrained-only) models may be MORE diverse than their instruction-tuned versions, because alignment/SFT on overlapping instruction datasets pulls models toward the same response style. If so, the very process meant to make models helpful/safe creates the hivemind.

**Direction:** Pair several open base models with their official instruction-tuned counterparts. On fixed open-ended prompts, measure inter-model homogeneity within the base set vs. within the instruct set. Test whether instruction tuning increases cross-model similarity (homogenization-by-alignment).

**Why it matters:** If alignment is a homogenization force, there is a real tension between safety tuning and diversity — a deeper root-cause finding for the hivemind. No training needed; both base and instruct checkpoints are public.

**Relevant context:** Targets the Artificial Hivemind root-cause open problem ('what causes output convergence'). Uses public base+instruct open checkpoints on a consumer GPU.

title: Correlated value blind spots: do models share the same omissions in moral/ethical reasoning?
quick_reasoning: Shared moral omission blind spots, diffuse long-horizon safety risk, well targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Correlated value blind spots: do models share the same omissions in moral/ethical reasoning?

**Problem:** Homogeneity of *values* is a fuzzy-reward, hard-to-measure failure mode that labs under-invest in. If diverse models systematically omit the same considerations when reasoning about ethical dilemmas (same neglected stakeholders, same ignored harms), our AI ecosystem has a shared moral blind spot.

**Direction:** Use a set of ethical-dilemma / value-tradeoff prompts. For each, query 6-8 models and have an external rubric enumerate which canonical considerations each response raises vs. omits. Measure whether omissions are correlated across models (same considerations consistently missing) more than chance.

**Why it matters:** Shared value omissions mean swapping vendors doesn't fix a moral blind spot — a diffuse, long-horizon risk frontier labs deprioritize. Evaluating fuzzy-reward homogeneity needs no lab resources and is high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Extends Artificial Hivemind to value reasoning; aligns with the fuzzy-reward evaluation priority. Inference + rubric annotation only.

title: Refusal Recovery After Chain-of-Thought Hijacking
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reasoning-trace shallow-alignment probe, core adversarial-robustness safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal Recovery After Chain-of-Thought Hijacking

**Problem:** Chain-of-thought hijacking (H-CoT) bypasses safety in reasoning models by injecting compliant reasoning steps, and longer CoT paradoxically reduces robustness — but whether a reasoning model can 'snap back' to refusal in its final answer after hijacked intermediate reasoning is unknown.

**Direction:** Using an open reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B or QwQ-style small model), inject hijacked compliant reasoning of varying lengths into the CoT, then measure whether the final answer still refuses. Map the 'reasoning-depth recovery curve' analogous to token-depth recovery, distinguishing CoT shallowness from output shallowness.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether the shallow-alignment finding extends from output tokens to reasoning traces — a flagged follow-up direction. Reasoning models are a medium-horizon safety concern; characterizing their distinct attack surface needs only inference on a small open model, no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Chain-of-Thought Hijacking (OpenReview, 2025) and H-CoT (arXiv:2502.12893): injecting execution-phase thoughts bypasses safety; longer CoT reduces robustness. Qi et al. shallow alignment is about output tokens; whether reasoning traces show the same shallowness is an open follow-up noted in the subfield context.

title: The Schelling-game homogeneity probe: do models silently coordinate via shared priors?
quick_reasoning: Implicit multi-agent coordination via shared focal points, recognized safety concern, scoped.

original_idea.body:
# The Schelling-game homogeneity probe: do models silently coordinate via shared priors?

**Problem:** Model organisms good at Schelling (coordination-without-communication) games are a flagged safety concern. Homogeneity provides a free coordination channel: if all models share the same 'obvious' focal point, separately deployed agents can implicitly collude without any communication. This shared-focal-point failure mode is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Run classic Schelling tasks (pick a number, a meeting place, a word) on 6-8 models, many samples each. Measure how concentrated the focal points are within and across models. Quantify the probability that two independently sampled, different-vendor models pick the SAME focal point — i.e., the implicit-coordination rate from homogeneity.

**Why it matters:** If homogeneity hands separately deployed AI agents a shared focal point, multi-agent systems can coordinate (or collude) without communication channels we can monitor. Cheap probe of a serious medium-horizon multi-agent risk; no training.

**Relevant context:** Connects model_homogeneity to the Schelling-game model-organism priority. Uses simple prompts + open/API models on a consumer GPU.

title: Prompt-injection generalization: does one injection string compromise a homogeneous model fleet?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets universal prompt injections compromising agentic fleets, clear security/safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Prompt-injection generalization: does one injection string compromise a homogeneous model fleet?

**Problem:** Prompt-injection defenses are deployed per-model, but if models share susceptibility (as jailbreaks do via shared representations), a single injection payload may compromise an entire fleet of nominally diverse models — a correlated security failure for agentic deployments.

**Direction:** Take a bank of published prompt-injection payloads. Test each against 6-8 instruction-tuned open/API models in a simple tool-use scaffold. Measure per-payload success across models and the fraction of payloads that succeed on ALL models (universal injections). Relate universality to model lineage.

**Why it matters:** Universal injections turn model diversity into security theater. Demonstrating their prevalence warns agentic-system builders that vendor diversity does not equal attack-surface diversity — directly actionable, infrastructure-free.

**Relevant context:** Builds on jailbreak-transfer-from-shared-representations (2506.12913) extended to prompt injection. Public payloads + open models; no training.

title: Diversity metric audit: which homogeneity measures actually detect safety-relevant convergence?
quick_reasoning: Foundational methodological audit ensuring homogeneity metrics track safety convergence, relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Diversity metric audit: which homogeneity measures actually detect safety-relevant convergence?

**Problem:** Homogeneity is reported via various metrics (embedding cosine similarity, n-gram overlap, distinct-n, self-BLEU). It is unclear which metrics detect *safety-relevant* convergence (shared wrong answers, shared refusals) vs. merely surface-style similarity — a methodological failure that could make homogeneity studies measure the wrong thing.

**Direction:** On a dataset with both surface-similar-but-semantically-diverse outputs and surface-different-but-semantically-identical outputs (constructed via paraphrase), compute several homogeneity metrics. Score each metric on how well it tracks ground-truth semantic/safety convergence. Recommend a robust metric and flag misleading ones.

**Why it matters:** Gives the emerging homogeneity subfield a vetted measurement toolkit so future work (and regulators) don't over- or under-state monoculture risk. A small but foundational methodological contribution requiring no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Methodological audit of the diversity metrics used in Artificial Hivemind and ensemble-diversity work. Embedding computation + paraphrase generation on a consumer GPU.

title: Quantization-induced failure correlation: do quantized variants of a model break identically?
quick_reasoning: Correlated quantized-variant failures as supply-chain homogeneity risk, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Quantization-induced failure correlation: do quantized variants of a model break identically?

**Problem:** Deployers run quantized (4-bit/8-bit) versions of open models for cost. If quantization introduces failures that are correlated across the whole quantization family (same prompts break at every bit-width), then the 'diversity' of model size/precision options is illusory for failure coverage.

**Direction:** Take one open model at full precision plus its 8-bit and 4-bit quantizations. On an error-prone prompt set, measure where each precision fails and test whether failures are shared across precisions vs. introduced independently. Repeat for a second model family to check generality.

**Why it matters:** Reveals whether the precision axis of model choice adds real failure diversity or just shared, inherited blind spots — a concrete supply-chain homogeneity question relevant to cheap, widespread deployments. Runs easily on a single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Connects model_homogeneity correlated-failure framing to quantization. Uses public quantized checkpoints (GGUF/bitsandbytes); inference only.

title: Reproducibility of the homogeneity effect: does it hold on a fresh, non-Infinity-Chat prompt set?
quick_reasoning: Replication hygiene for homogeneity effect; safety relevance present but indirect/foundational.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducibility of the homogeneity effect: does it hold on a fresh, non-Infinity-Chat prompt set?

**Problem:** A best-paper result should replicate on independent data. The hivemind effect was established on Infinity-Chat; an out-of-distribution replication on a fresh, independently collected open-ended prompt set is needed to rule out dataset-specific artifacts before the community builds on it.

**Direction:** Collect a fresh ~200-prompt open-ended set from a different source (e.g., public forum questions, a different taxonomy). Run the paper's diversity metrics on 8-10 models and compare effect sizes to the published Infinity-Chat numbers. Report whether homogeneity magnitude replicates and where it differs.

**Why it matters:** Independent replication is foundational hygiene for an emerging subfield and is exactly the kind of careful, resource-light work academia should do. Confirming (or qualifying) the headline effect strengthens the whole research program.

**Relevant context:** Direct replication of Artificial Hivemind (OpenReview saDOrrnNTz) on out-of-distribution prompts, reusing its public metrics. Inference + embeddings on a consumer GPU.

title: Does retrieval break the hivemind, or share it? RAG-grounded homogeneity test
quick_reasoning: Tests whether shared RAG amplifies monoculture in high-stakes answers, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Does retrieval break the hivemind, or share it? RAG-grounded homogeneity test

**Problem:** RAG is promoted as a way to make model outputs more grounded and varied. But if diverse models retrieve and copy the same passages, RAG could INCREASE inter-model homogeneity (everyone parrots the top retrieved chunk) — a counterintuitive failure mode for grounded safety-critical answers.

**Direction:** Build a small shared corpus + retriever. Answer a fixed query set with and without RAG across several models. Measure inter-model output similarity in both conditions. Test whether shared retrieval homogenizes answers more than ungrounded generation does.

**Why it matters:** If shared retrieval pipelines amplify monoculture, the rush to RAG-everything in high-stakes settings quietly concentrates risk. A clean, surprising-result-style finding with a small reusable RAG harness; no training.

**Relevant context:** Extends model_homogeneity to retrieval-augmented setups; uses an open retriever + open models on a consumer GPU.

title: Multilingual blind-spot transfer: are shared failures replicated across languages?
quick_reasoning: Language-invariant shared blind spots as global deployment risk, well targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Multilingual blind-spot transfer: are shared failures replicated across languages?

**Problem:** The hivemind has been studied mostly in English. If models share blind spots in English AND those same conceptual blind spots reappear across languages, the monoculture is deeper than a training-data-language artifact and harder to escape by switching locales.

**Direction:** Translate a set of safety/factual probe items into 3-4 languages. Query several multilingual open models. Measure (a) per-language correlated failure across models and (b) whether the SAME conceptual items fail across languages within and across models. Characterize language-invariant shared blind spots.

**Why it matters:** Language-invariant shared blind spots mean global deployments inherit the same gaps everywhere — a diffuse, under-studied risk for non-English-speaking populations that labs deprioritize. Inference-only, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Extends shared-blind-spot framing across languages; uses open multilingual models + public translation. No training.

title: Confidence homogeneity: do models share the same miscalibration on the same items?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets correlated overconfidence defeating confidence-based safety filters.

original_idea.body:
# Confidence homogeneity: do models share the same miscalibration on the same items?

**Problem:** Beyond sharing wrong answers, models may share *overconfidence* on the same items. If diverse models are all confidently wrong on the same prompts, confidence-based abstention/escalation (a common safety control) fails simultaneously across the fleet — a correlated calibration failure.

**Direction:** On a labeled QA set, elicit verbalized or logit-based confidence from several models. Identify high-confidence-wrong items per model and test whether these items overlap across models more than chance. Map the shared 'confidently wrong' region.

**Why it matters:** Confidence thresholds are a frontline safety filter; if overconfidence is correlated, raising the bar doesn't help because every model is equally fooled on the same items. Demonstrates a correlated calibration blind spot with only inference + stats.

**Relevant context:** Combines calibration literature with model_homogeneity correlated-failure framing. Open/API models on a consumer GPU.

title: Paraphrase-collapse: do diverse models map different questions onto the same answer template?
quick_reasoning: Shared interpretive homogeneity blind spot, safety-relevant though subtler.

original_idea.body:
# Paraphrase-collapse: do diverse models map different questions onto the same answer template?

**Problem:** Ensembling-diversity work (arXiv 2507.21168) asks whether diversity comes from models or from question interpretations. A specific failure mode: many distinct user phrasings collapse onto one canonical answer across all models, so the system is blind to nuance the phrasing intended — shared interpretive homogeneity.

**Direction:** Take a set of base questions and generate multiple paraphrases each (varying intent subtly). Query several models. Measure within-model and cross-model answer collapse: how often do semantically-different paraphrases produce near-identical answers, and is the collapse shared across models?

**Why it matters:** If every model ignores phrasing nuance the same way, users cannot route around the blind spot by rephrasing or switching vendors — a subtle, shared interpretive failure. Cheap to run, directly extends a recent ensembling paper.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on 'Diverse LLMs or Diverse Question Interpretations?' (arXiv 2507.21168). Paraphrase generation + inference on a consumer GPU.

title: Self-correction blind spot as a shared failure: do models all fail to fix the same mistakes?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets correlated self-correction blind spot undermining self-critique safety loops.

original_idea.body:
# Self-correction blind spot as a shared failure: do models all fail to fix the same mistakes?

**Problem:** Self-Correction Bench (arXiv 2507.02778) found a self-correction blind spot. If this blind spot is shared — models all fail to self-correct on the SAME error types — then self-critique safety loops have a correlated, fleet-wide gap that swapping models won't close.

**Direction:** Use the self-correction probe paradigm: present each model with its own (or a fixed) erroneous answer and prompt it to revise. Measure correction success per model per item, then test whether the items models FAIL to self-correct overlap across models more than chance. Characterize the shared uncorrectable region.

**Why it matters:** Self-critique is a popular cheap safety mechanism; a correlated self-correction blind spot means it fails the same way everywhere. Demonstrating this scopes the limits of self-critique with no training and modest compute.

**Relevant context:** Grounds on Self-Correction Bench (arXiv 2507.02778) combined with model_homogeneity correlated-failure analysis. Inference + overlap statistics.

title: Activation Probe Stability Under Distribution Shift of Benign Inputs
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped false-positive stress test of jailbreak-detection probes, core adversarial-robustness deployment problem.

original_idea.body:
# Activation Probe Stability Under Distribution Shift of Benign Inputs

**Problem:** Activation-probe jailbreak detectors achieve high recall at low false-positive rates, but their false-positive behavior has been tested mostly on standard benign prompts; whether they spuriously fire on unusual-but-benign domains (medical, legal, fiction, code) — a deployment-critical failure — is untested.

**Direction:** Train a simple logistic-regression probe on a published jailbreak dataset's activations from one open model, then stress-test its false-positive rate across diverse benign corpora (clinical notes, legal text, dark fiction, security CTF writeups). Report which benign domains trigger spurious detections.

**Why it matters:** Bridging lab-tested defenses to real deployment robustness is a stated open problem. Over-refusal from probe false positives is a silent harm. This is a cheap, no-training, infrastructure-light evaluation that yields a reusable benign stress-test suite — high counterfactual value outside labs.

**Relevant context:** Activation probes detect jailbreaks at ~90% recall, 1% FPR (subfield context; arXiv:2411.09003 affine refusal). Over-refusal literature (XSTest, OR-Bench arXiv:2405.20947) shows lexical overfitting causes false refusals on benign sensitive-keyword prompts; whether probes inherit this is unstudied.

# Hill Numbers for LLM Output Diversity: An Ecology-Borrowed Effective-Diversity Metric

**Problem:** The Artificial Hivemind paper documents inter-model homogeneity but mostly uses ad-hoc similarity scores. There is no principled, sample-size-robust, single-axis metric that lets you say 'these N models behave like an effective community of k_eff distinct responders' on a safety-relevant query.

**Direction:** Import Hill numbers (the unifying diversity framework from ecology that subsumes richness, Shannon, and Simpson as a tunable order-q family) and apply them to a bag of LLM responses. Embed responses (Sentence-BERT), cluster into 'response species,' compute Hill diversity of order 0/1/2 across a panel of ~6-10 open models on a slice of Infinity-Chat plus safety-flavored prompts (refusal-edge cases, advice questions). Report effective number of distinct response modes and how it collapses as you move from q=0 (richness) to q=2 (dominance-weighted).

**Why it matters:** A standardized effective-diversity number makes correlated-failure risk measurable and comparable across model panels, which is exactly the monitoring gap flagged for systemic/concentration risk. Ecologists already solved the rare-vs-common-species and sample-coverage problems that plague naive distinct-n-gram metrics, so the transfer is high-leverage.

**Relevant context:** Hill numbers unify Shannon/Simpson/richness as order-q diversity (Roswell 2021 Oikos; Broms 2015 Methods Ecol Evol). Artificial Hivemind / Infinity-Chat (NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper, arXiv:2510.22954). Diversity metrics for LLMs use Sentence-BERT cosine and distinct-n (arXiv:2310.06452).

# Diversity Prediction Theorem as a Safety Audit for Multi-Model Aggregation

**Problem:** When several LLMs vote/average on a factual or risk judgment, the quality of the aggregate is governed (per cognitive science) by collective error = average individual error minus diversity. Homogeneous models have low diversity, so aggregation buys little. No one has measured the diversity term empirically for LLM panels on safety judgments.

**Direction:** Apply Surowiecki/Page's Diversity Prediction Theorem decomposition directly. On numeric-estimate safety tasks (probability a statement is true, harmfulness on a 0-10 scale, calibration questions) with ground truth, run a model panel, and empirically decompose collective squared error into average-individual-error and predictive-diversity components. Show how much of the potential crowd benefit homogeneity has already eaten.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies, in a single interpretable equation, how model homogeneity undermines the 'wisdom of model crowds' that aggregation-based safety schemes rely on. Lab-independent, theoretically grounded, and directly tied to correlated-failure risk.

**Relevant context:** Diversity Prediction Theorem: collective error = average error - diversity (Surowiecki 2004; Page). Wisdom-of-crowds conditions require diversity+independence. Artificial Hivemind homogeneity (arXiv:2510.22954).

**Why it matters:** Gives a concrete, contagion-style metric for cascading failures across systems sharing a model lineage, and tests heterogeneity as a 'herd immunity' mitigation — directly addressing the cascading-failure open problem with a vivid, lab-independent experiment.

Demonstrate transitive correlated risk.

**Why it matters:** Builds prototype monitoring infrastructure for concentration/supply-chain risk that maps and tests shared dependencies — exactly the systemic-risk monitoring gap, achievable with public metadata and small open models.

**Relevant context:** SBOM / software supply-chain dependency auditing from cybersecurity. HuggingFace fine-tune lineage; PhyloLM lineage clustering (arXiv:2404.04671). Concentration/cascading-failure open problems (context file).

original_idea.body:
# Antifragility Stress-Testing: Does Adding Models Reduce or Concentrate Tail Risk?

**Problem:** Taleb's framework distinguishes systems that are fragile, robust, or antifragile to volatility, and warns that naive diversification can hide fat-tailed concentration. Whether scaling up a model panel reduces tail risk (rare catastrophic all-models-wrong events) or merely hides it is unstudied with this lens.

**Direction:** Borrow fat-tail/tail-risk stress-testing methodology. Estimate the tail of the 'fraction of panel simultaneously wrong' distribution on hard safety judgments, and test whether adding more (homogeneous) models thins or fattens the tail of catastrophic joint errors. Compare homogeneous-scaling vs lineage-diverse-scaling.

**Why it matters:** Challenges the intuition that 'more models = safer' by examining tail behavior, the part that matters for catastrophe. Directly addresses correlated catastrophic failure with an established risk-analysis toolkit, no lab resources needed.

**Relevant context:** Fat-tails / antifragility / tail-risk concentration (Taleb). Correlation breakdown under stress (arXiv:1312.0506). Artificial Hivemind correlated failures (arXiv:2510.22954).
